title: Purpose of hand hygiene
content: Hand hygiene is a foundational infection-prevention practice. Its educational purpose is to reduce the transfer of microorganisms between people, surfaces, and care activities. Learners should connect the practice to risk reduction rather than treating it as a memorized ritual.

title: Choosing a hand hygiene method
content: Educational guidance commonly distinguishes washing with soap and water from using an alcohol-based hand rub. The appropriate method depends on visible soil, the care context, and current institutional policy. A study answer should explain the reasoning and refer to local requirements.

title: Hand hygiene timing
content: Hand hygiene is considered before and after care activities when hands may transmit microorganisms. Learners should identify transitions in activity, contact with the environment, and changes from contaminated to cleaner tasks. Exact timing language should be checked against the learner's approved policy.

title: Gloves and hand hygiene
content: Gloves are a barrier but do not replace hand hygiene. Gloves may have defects, hands may become contaminated during removal, and organisms may transfer when the same gloves are used across tasks. Learners should treat glove use and hand hygiene as related but separate practices.

title: Hand care and technique quality
content: Skin condition, jewelry, nails, product access, and workload can affect hand-hygiene quality. A learning review should consider both the technical action and the system conditions that make reliable practice easier or harder.

title: PPE risk assessment
content: Personal protective equipment selection begins with a risk assessment. The learner considers the expected exposure route, the task, the environment, and current policy. PPE should not be selected only from the name of a procedure.

title: PPE categories
content: Common PPE categories include gloves, gowns, masks or respirators, and eye or face protection. Each protects against a different exposure pathway. A strong study response links the equipment to the anticipated risk.

title: Principle of putting on PPE
content: When studying how PPE is put on, focus on preparing equipment, checking fit and integrity, and avoiding contamination of clothing or skin. Exact sequences can vary by equipment and institution, so learners should compare the concept with their approved checklist.

title: Principle of removing PPE
content: PPE removal is studied as a contamination-control process. Learners should identify which surfaces may be contaminated, minimize contact with those surfaces, and perform hand hygiene at policy-defined points. The exact removal sequence must follow the approved local procedure.

title: Masks and respirators
content: Masks and respirators are not interchangeable. Educational review should distinguish source control, splash protection, filtration, fit, and seal requirements. Device selection and use must follow current institutional and occupational-health policy.

title: Eye and face protection
content: Eye or face protection is considered when splashes, sprays, or droplets may reach mucous membranes. Learners should be able to explain the exposure pathway and how the selected barrier addresses it.

title: Limits of PPE
content: PPE is one layer of protection and does not replace hand hygiene, environmental controls, safe work practices, or correct equipment handling. Study answers should avoid presenting PPE as a complete solution by itself.

title: Clean and sterile technique
content: Clean technique aims to reduce microorganisms, while sterile technique aims to maintain an area and items free from viable microorganisms according to the approved procedure. Learners should describe the different goals rather than only memorizing labels.

title: Sterile field awareness
content: A sterile field is managed by continuously observing it and controlling what enters it. Items are treated according to their verified status, packaging, integrity, and the rules in the approved procedure.

title: Recognizing contamination
content: In educational scenarios, contamination may occur when sterility is uncertain, packaging is compromised, an item contacts a non-sterile surface, or the field is left unobserved contrary to policy. When in doubt, the learner should consult the approved procedure rather than improvise.

title: Movement around a sterile field
content: Movement can create opportunities for contact, airflow disruption, or loss of field awareness. Learners should plan supplies and positioning before beginning and avoid unnecessary movement. Specific boundaries and distances are policy-dependent.

title: Moisture and barrier integrity
content: Moisture can affect barrier integrity and may allow transfer through materials. Learners should inspect the field and supplies for wetness or damage and follow the institution's rule for replacing compromised items.

title: Preparing sterile supplies
content: Preparation includes confirming the correct supplies, checking package integrity and expiry information, organizing the workspace, and reviewing the approved procedure before beginning. The goal is to reduce interruptions and uncertainty.

title: SBAR overview
content: SBAR is a structured communication framework: Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation. It helps organize important information so the receiver can understand the immediate concern, relevant context, the speaker's assessment, and the requested next step.

title: SBAR situation
content: The Situation section states why the communication is occurring now. It should be concise and identify the main concern without a long history.

title: SBAR background
content: The Background section provides only the context needed to understand the current concern. Learners should prioritize relevant facts and avoid unrelated detail.

title: SBAR assessment
content: The Assessment section communicates what the speaker has observed and how the information is understood within the speaker's role. A learner should separate observed facts from assumptions and remain within scope.

title: SBAR recommendation
content: The Recommendation section states what response, clarification, review, or action is being requested. A clear recommendation reduces ambiguity and supports closed-loop communication.

title: Closed-loop communication
content: Closed-loop communication confirms that a message was received and understood. Read-back, clarification, and confirmation can reduce errors when information is complex or urgent. Exact organizational expectations should follow policy.

title: Objective documentation
content: Objective documentation describes observations, actions, and responses using specific, neutral language. Learners should avoid judgmental labels, unsupported conclusions, or vague wording.

title: Timely documentation
content: Timely documentation supports continuity and reduces reliance on memory. When an entry cannot be completed at the expected time, learners should follow the approved process rather than altering timestamps or concealing the delay.

title: Documentation corrections
content: Corrections must preserve the integrity of the record. Learners should use the approved electronic or paper correction process and should never erase, obscure, or silently replace an original entry.

title: Approved abbreviations
content: Abbreviations can be misunderstood. Learners should use only abbreviations approved by their institution and write terms in full when uncertain.

title: Privacy in documentation
content: Documentation should include information relevant to care while protecting privacy. Access, discussion, copying, and disposal of records are governed by organizational policy and applicable law. This study app should never receive real patient identifiers.

title: Incident reports and the clinical record
content: An incident-reporting process and the clinical record serve different purposes. Learners should follow policy for each and avoid copying confidential internal analysis into the clinical record unless required by the approved process.

title: Retrieval practice
content: Retrieval practice means trying to recall information before looking at the answer. Short quizzes, blank-page summaries, and explaining a concept aloud can reveal gaps more effectively than rereading alone.

title: Spaced review
content: Spaced review revisits material across multiple sessions rather than concentrating all study into one period. The spacing can be adjusted based on difficulty and performance.

title: Deliberate practice
content: Deliberate practice targets a specific weak skill, uses a clear success criterion, and includes feedback. Repeating an entire routine without identifying errors is less efficient.

title: Error log
content: An error log records the question or skill, the incorrect idea, the corrected explanation, and a plan to prevent repetition. Reviewing the log turns mistakes into study targets.

title: Self-explanation
content: Self-explanation asks the learner to explain why a step or principle matters. This links actions to reasoning and makes it easier to adapt knowledge to a new scenario.

title: Simulation reflection
content: After a fictional simulation, reflection can examine what happened, what cues were noticed, what communication worked, and what should be practised next. Reflection is for learning and does not certify competence.
